question.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$ 

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 4 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Since all of the eigenvalues are simple roots of the characteristic polynomial, $A$ is diagonalizable.  

We construct a diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal. Therefore, one possible matrix $D$ is 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Note that the diagonal matrix $D$ is unique up to the ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore, another possible matrix diagonal matrix is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$
